name: Diana Harshbarger
bio: Two-term incumbent first elected 2020. Trump-endorsed; expected to win re-nomination handily.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: Rep. Harshbarger supports school choice and parental rights in education, emphasizing state and local control over K-12 decisions. No specific public statements supporting or opposing Head Start or federal pre-K funding were found as of July 2026.
early_childhood_ed.details: As a member of the House Committee on Education and Labor, Harshbarger has consistently advocated for school choice, educational freedom, and limiting federal government involvement in K-12 education. Her official education page states: 'I strongly support school choice and educational freedoms. Students and their families should be empowered with the freedom to choose their own educational pathways.' She co-sponsored H.R. 6056, the Parents Bill of Rights Act, to require curriculum transparency and parental access to school information. She has not published specific positions on Head Start or federal pre-K expansion. No public statements on childcare costs or childcare tax credits were found as of July 2026.

child_hunger.summary: Rep. Harshbarger voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (May 22, 2025), which enacted significant SNAP funding cuts and added new work requirements. She separately introduced a 2026 bill focused on nutrition education at community health centers.
child_hunger.details: On May 22, 2025, Harshbarger issued a statement: 'I voted YES for President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, and I'm proud to stand with the President.' The One Big Beautiful Bill Act cut approximately $186 billion from SNAP nationally, added expanded work and school requirements for eligibility, and shifted a portion of benefit costs to states. As reported in June 2026, about 100,000 Tennesseans lost SNAP benefits after the law took effect in July 2025, with statewide SNAP enrollment falling 14.35% by March 2026. Separately, in June 2026 Harshbarger introduced the Nutrition Education and Chronic Disease Prevention in Community Health Centers Act of 2026, which would fund nutrition counseling and education at federally qualified health centers, with priority for communities with high rates of food insecurity and diet-related disease. This bill targets prevention at health centers, not direct food assistance for children.

parental_support.summary: Rep. Harshbarger co-sponsored the Parents Bill of Rights Act (H.R. 6056), which focuses on curriculum transparency and parental involvement in schools. She voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended Child Tax Credit provisions. No public positions on paid family leave were found as of July 2026.
parental_support.details: Harshbarger co-sponsored H.R. 6056, the Parents Bill of Rights Act, requiring full online curriculum transparency and giving parents access to information about what is taught in their child's school. In her statement on the One Big Beautiful Bill (May 22, 2025), she cited it as extending '2017 tax cuts for hardworking families,' which included Child Tax Credit provisions. She also applauded the U.S. Supreme Court's 2025 ruling upholding Tennessee's law prohibiting gender transition procedures for minors. No public statements specifically addressing paid family leave or childcare subsidies were found as of July 2026.

name: Kristi Burke
bio: Democratic primary candidate from East Tennessee.
photo_credit: Direct headshot URL not found; campaign uses logo imagery

early_childhood_ed.summary: Kristi Burke's campaign platform calls for expanding early childhood education and fully funding public education from early childhood through higher education, while opposing private school voucher programs that divert public school funds.
early_childhood_ed.details: On her campaign website's non-negotiables page, Burke states that 'Public education is essential to opportunity, economic mobility, and a functioning democracy. Public dollars must go to public schools, and education must be accessible from early childhood through higher education.' Her plan includes: 'Fully fund public education,' 'Expand early childhood education,' 'Provide universal school meals,' 'Restore and strengthen the U.S. Department of Education,' and 'Protect and expand Title I.' She criticizes Tennessee's private school voucher programs, noting that 'An estimated 70% of the vouchers dished out in 2026 went to students already enrolled in private schools.' She also calls for fully funding IDEA (special education) and expanding school-based mental health services.

child_hunger.summary: Burke's platform supports universal school meals and fully funded public education that includes nutrition access, but no specific statements on SNAP expansion or WIC were found as of July 2026.
child_hunger.details: On Burke's non-negotiables page, her education plan includes 'Provide universal school meals,' reflecting a position that all students should have access to no-cost meals at school. Her campaign broadly supports shifting tax burdens from working families to corporations and reinvesting in community safety nets and schools. In a June 2026 community event, she stated: 'We need to make sure that we're lifting everyone up from the bottom and taking care of our basic needs.' However, no specific public statements on SNAP eligibility, WIC, or the One Big Beautiful Bill's SNAP cuts were found on her campaign website or in news coverage as of July 2026.

parental_support.summary: Burke supports Medicare for All, fully funded public education, and tax fairness for working families, but no specific positions on paid family leave or the Child Tax Credit were found as of July 2026.
parental_support.details: Burke's campaign non-negotiables state that healthcare is a human right and she supports 'a universal, single-payer system. Medicare for All would ensure every person is covered, regardless of income, job, or circumstance.' She advocates cutting taxes for working families and shifting the tax burden to wealthy individuals and corporations. On reproductive rights, she supports protecting access to contraception and abortion. She describes herself as renting her home and lacking health insurance — framing her campaign as a fight for 'a future where every family has a fair shot at a stable, dignified life.' No public positions specifically addressing paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare subsidies were found as of July 2026.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Herman Garcia has made Universal Pre-K a central campaign priority, calling for free, high-quality pre-K for all 3- and 4-year-olds, capping childcare costs at 7% of a working family's income, and investing in early childhood educator wages.
early_childhood_ed.details: Garcia's campaign issues page states: 'Early childhood education is critical for a child's cognitive and social development. Yet, the skyrocketing cost of childcare and preschool is bankrupting working families in East Tennessee. Universal Pre-K ensures every child gets a head start while giving parents the financial relief they need to participate fully in our local economy.' His specific action plan includes: 'Provide free, high-quality Pre-K for all 3 and 4-year-olds,' 'Cap childcare costs at 7% of a working family's income,' and 'Invest in early childhood educators with competitive, living wages.'

child_hunger.summary: Garcia explicitly supports expanding SNAP benefits, eliminating unnecessary restrictions on the program, supporting community food banks, and ensuring living wages so families can afford nutritious food.
child_hunger.details: Garcia's campaign issues page includes a dedicated 'Food Insecurity' section stating: 'In the wealthiest nation on Earth, families in East Tennessee are choosing between buying groceries and paying rent. Food insecurity is a crisis that affects children, seniors, and working families who do everything right but still can't afford to eat.' His action plan includes: 'Expand SNAP benefits and eliminate unnecessary restrictions,' 'Support community food banks and local agricultural initiatives,' and 'Ensure living wages so families can afford nutritious food.' His BallotReady profile also confirms support for expanding nutrition assistance programs.

parental_support.summary: Garcia supports Universal Pre-K as parental financial relief, a $15/hour federal minimum wage, universal healthcare, and progressive tax reform to benefit working families, though no specific positions on paid family leave or the Child Tax Credit were found as of July 2026.
parental_support.details: Garcia's campaign platform frames Universal Pre-K explicitly as a parental support measure: it 'ensures every child gets a head start while giving parents the financial relief they need to participate fully in our local economy.' His minimum wage proposal calls for raising the federal minimum wage to $15 per hour indexed to inflation, with small business tax credits during the transition. His universal healthcare position argues that 'tying healthcare to employment leaves millions vulnerable.' No specific positions on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit as a standalone policy, or childcare tax subsidies beyond the Universal Pre-K cost-cap proposal were found as of July 2026.

early_childhood_ed.details: David Kerr's official campaign website and his responses to the Knox News voter guide (July 16, 2026) do not contain specific positions on early childhood education, Head Start, pre-K access, childcare costs, or childcare tax credits. His platform emphasizes rural healthcare access, term limits, lobbying reform, and constituent-first representation. He supports 'initiatives that benefit working families and rural economies' broadly but has not published specific early childhood education proposals.

child_hunger.details: No public statements on child hunger, SNAP benefits, school nutrition programs, WIC, or food insecurity were found for David Kerr on his campaign website, in his Knox News voter guide interview (July 16, 2026), or in other available news sources as of July 2026. His campaign's stated priorities center on rural healthcare infrastructure, government accountability, term limits, and constituent representation.

parental_support.summary: Kerr supports protecting access to reproductive and maternal healthcare. No specific positions on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or childcare subsidies were found as of July 2026.
parental_support.details: Kerr's campaign platform includes a Women's Health section stating he supports protecting 'access to comprehensive reproductive healthcare, including family planning and maternal care' and that 'personal medical decisions should be made by individuals, their families, and their doctors — not politicians.' He also states that women in rural communities deserve access to essential healthcare services. His Knox News voter guide response called for a progressive 'fair share' tax system. name: Tim Burchett
bio: Three-term incumbent serving since 2019. Outspoken populist conservative; minimal primary opposition.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: Rep. Burchett advocates abolishing the U.S. Department of Education and returning education authority to states and localities. He supports school choice and parental choice but has expressed concern about the impact of voucher programs on rural communities that lack private schools.
early_childhood_ed.details: Burchett's official education page states: 'I come from a family of educators, and I believe our federal government is not properly equipped to make decisions about schools and teaching across the United States. We should abolish the Department of Education and return authority back to state and local governments.' In February 2025, he reintroduced H.R. 847, the Building Lasting Opportunities for Community K-12 (BLOCK) Act. He told WBIR in January 2025 that he is concerned about how universal school voucher legislation will impact rural communities: 'I worry about the kids in some of our rural communities and I hope we address some of their problems.' He introduced H.R. 8465, the Funding Early Childhood is the Right IDEA Act. No specific Head Start or pre-K expansion positions were found as of July 2026.

child_hunger.summary: Rep. Burchett voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which enacted major SNAP cuts and new work requirements. When a government shutdown in fall 2025 threatened SNAP benefits for over 55,000 of his constituents, his office said there was little he could do and blamed Senate Democrats for the shutdown.
child_hunger.details: At least 55,758 people in Burchett's TN-2 district relied on SNAP as of September 2025. During a federal government shutdown in fall 2025, when SNAP benefits were at risk in November, Burchett's spokesman Will Garrett told the Knoxville News Sentinel: 'It's unfortunate that the Democrats' government shutdown is impacting so many hardworking East Tennesseans' and added that 'until Democrats in the Senate vote to end the shutdown, the support our casework team can provide is limited.' Burchett voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut approximately $186 billion from SNAP nationally, added and expanded work and school requirements for recipients, and shifted a portion of benefit costs to states. The law took effect July 2025, and by March 2026 SNAP enrollment in Tennessee had fallen 14.35%.

parental_support.summary: Rep. Burchett supports school choice and parental rights in education, and voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act which extended certain tax provisions including Child Tax Credit elements. No specific positions on paid family leave or childcare subsidies were found as of July 2026.
parental_support.details: Burchett supports school choice and parental rights in education decisions, though he has expressed concern about voucher programs' impact on rural areas. He voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which extended the 2017 tax cuts including Child Tax Credit provisions, while also cutting social safety net programs. In January 2026, he was named chair of the DOGE Subcommittee focused on reducing government spending. His education focus has been on the BLOCK Act (H.R. 847) and the Educators Expense Deduction Modernization Act. No public statements specifically on paid family leave, childcare subsidies, or the Child Tax Credit as standalone policy were found as of July 2026.

name: Chuck Fleischmann
bio: Eight-term incumbent and Chattanooga attorney. $4.1M cash on hand; expected easy re-nomination.
photo_credit: U.S. House Office of the Clerk

early_childhood_ed.summary: Rep. Fleischmann sponsored H.R.8465, the 'Funding Early Childhood is the Right IDEA Act,' in the 119th Congress (2025-2026), reflecting engagement with early childhood education funding. His general education philosophy favors state rather than federal control.
early_childhood_ed.details: Fleischmann sponsored H.R.8465, the 'Funding Early Childhood is the Right IDEA Act' (119th Congress, 2025-2026), a bill aimed at funding early childhood education and childcare initiatives. His official education page states he believes 'education is best left to state governments' and that he opposes federal coercion of state education standards. As a senior Appropriations Committee member, Fleischmann also serves on the Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education Appropriations Subcommittee, which funds Head Start and related programs.

child_hunger.summary: During the 2025 government shutdown, Fleischmann publicly called the interruption to SNAP benefits 'outrageous' and advocated for restoring funding; he also voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which significantly restructured SNAP.
child_hunger.details: In November 2025, during a federal government shutdown, Rep. Fleischmann stated the halt to SNAP payments was 'This historic, unforgivable government shutdown has hurt poor people, hard-working people, and federal workers. It's outrageous. It's a failure of American government' (NewsChannel 9, Nov. 11, 2025). He advocated for a bipartisan measure to reopen the government and release SNAP benefits. However, his voting record also shows he voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R.1), which cut approximately $186 billion from SNAP nationwide and tightened work requirements. That law resulted in approximately 100,000 Tennesseans losing SNAP benefits since July 2025.

parental_support.summary: Fleischmann's voting record shows he did not cosponsor national paid family and medical leave legislation, and voted in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill which defunded Planned Parenthood; no specific public positions on the Child Tax Credit were found.
parental_support.details: According to YourRepRecord.org voting record data (119th Congress), Fleischmann failed to cosponsor H.R.5390, the national paid family and medical leave bill. He voted YES on the One Big Beautiful Bill (H.R.1), which included defunding of Planned Parenthood. He also voted YES on a budget resolution enabling $880 billion in Medicaid cuts (H.Con.Res.14) and voted NO on extending ACA premium tax credits (H.R.1834). The OnTheIssues.org profile for Fleischmann lists 'No stance on record' under Families & Children. No specific statements on the Child Tax Credit or childcare subsidies for parents were identified in available 2025-2026 materials.

child_hunger.summary: DesJarlais has been a consistent supporter of SNAP work requirements throughout his congressional career, backing the One Big Beautiful Bill's SNAP restructuring, while also raising concerns about SNAP access by undocumented immigrants.
child_hunger.details: In a July 2025 interview, DesJarlais stated: 'As a member of the House Agriculture Committee, I've been supporting work requirements for able-bodied adults to receive SNAP benefits for my entire time in Congress. Two-thirds of all Americans across all political spectrums have consistently supported work requirements for food stamps in polling. The time is now to work to rein in this program back to what it was intended to be — temporary food assistance to those who need it to get back on their feet.' He supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut approximately $186 billion from SNAP and expanded work requirements up to age 64. In October 2025, DesJarlais authored a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem expressing concern about undocumented immigrants potentially accessing SNAP benefits.

parental_support.summary: DesJarlais voted YES on the Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women Act and the Protect Children's Innocence Act, and did not cosponsor national paid family and medical leave legislation.

name: Andy Ogles
bio: Two-term incumbent facing FEC violations and Ethics Committee scrutiny. Just $85K cash on hand (Q1 2026) — among the lowest of any U.S. House incumbent nationally. Trump-endorsed despite ongoing investigations.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Rep. Andy Ogles has not publicly championed early childhood education programs; his education-related statements have focused on school choice and arming teachers rather than pre-K or Head Start access.
early_childhood_ed.details: Rep. Andy Ogles (TN-5 incumbent) has not published specific statements in support of expanding Head Start, pre-K, or federal childcare programs. His congressional education page focuses primarily on higher education and K-12 issues such as armed teachers and immigration enforcement at universities. In April 2024 he applauded the Tennessee General Assembly's bill allowing trained teachers to carry concealed firearms on school campuses. The 'One Big Beautiful Bill' (H.R. 1) that Ogles voted for in July 2025 did not include provisions to expand Head Start. No public statements by Ogles specifically endorsing pre-K expansion, Head Start funding, or childcare assistance programs were found in available sources as of July 2026.

child_hunger.summary: Rep. Ogles voted in both May and July 2025 for the Republican reconciliation bill (the 'One Big Beautiful Bill'), which included the largest cuts to SNAP in the program's history, totaling $186 billion through 2034.
child_hunger.details: Rep. Andy Ogles voted for the House version of the FY 2025 Republican budget reconciliation bill in May 2025 (House Vote 145, passed 215-214), which included nearly $300 billion in cuts to SNAP. He also voted for the final Senate version in July 2025 (House Vote 190, passed 218-214), which cut SNAP by $186 billion through 2034 — described by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities as 'the largest cut to SNAP in history.' The bill expanded SNAP work requirements and shifted more benefit costs to states. According to FNS data cited by American Bridge, more than 14,000 Tennesseans in TN-5 relied on SNAP. As of March 2026, SNAP enrollment in Tennessee had decreased by 14.35% since July 2025.

parental_support.summary: Rep. Ogles voted for the 2025 Republican reconciliation bill, which included a temporary expansion of the Child Tax Credit and made permanent an employer paid family leave tax credit, while also cutting Medicaid and SNAP that many families depend on.
parental_support.details: The 'One Big Beautiful Bill' (H.R. 1) that Ogles voted for in both May and July 2025 included provisions to temporarily increase the Child Tax Credit and make permanent the Section 45S employer tax credit for paid family leave. However, the same legislation cut $186 billion from SNAP and reduced Medicaid, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated would cause 11.8 million people to lose insurance. Ogles has not published standalone statements on paid family leave, childcare subsidies, or maternal health policy. Democratic challenger Chaz Molder has highlighted Ogles's votes against extending Affordable Care Act subsidies, which resulted in approximately 70,000 Tennesseans losing Marketplace health insurance access.
